case.case_title: Dhanapala Fernando v. Attanayaka, Officer-in-Charge, Kandana Police Station and Others

clause.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the police searches and arrests at the licensed Inn violated the petitioner's fundamental right to equality and equal protection under Article 12(1) of the Constitution.
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioner claimed that the police conducted illegal searches and arbitrary arrests at his licensed business premises without reasonable suspicion or consent, infringing his fundamental rights under Article 12(1).
case_context.respondent_argument: The respondents argued that the searches and arrests were justified under sections 32 and 33 of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act and sections 65 and 68 of the Police Ordinance, based on suspicion of criminal or underworld activities and inability of guests to establish their identity.
key_facts: The petitioner owned a licensed restaurant and inn called Jayasiri Restaurant and Inn.
Police conducted multiple raids and searches on the premises without consent, allegedly at gunpoint.
Three couples and the Manager were arrested for failing to establish identity, but all had given names and addresses.
Police had no reasonable suspicion or credible information justifying the arrests or searches.
The business was effectively closed from 3 June 2002 until interim relief was granted on 25 June 2002.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The court held that Article 12(1) guarantees equality before the law and equal protection, which prohibits arbitrary and unjustified actions by the state such as unlawful searches and arrests without reasonable suspicion or consent.
reasoning.application_to_facts: The court found that the police failed to establish any factual basis or reasonable suspicion for the arrests or searches, that the searches were conducted without consent and by coercion, and that the actions were arbitrary and high-handed, thus violating the petitioner's fundamental rights under Article 12(1).
principles_established: Reasonable suspicion or credible information is required to justify arrests and searches under the law.
Police powers under the Code of Criminal Procedure and Police Ordinance do not authorize arbitrary or unjustified searches or arrests.
The right to equality before the law includes protection against arbitrary state action infringing personal liberty and privacy.

outcome.holding: The court held that the police searches and arrests violated the petitioner's fundamental right under Article 12(1) and declared the infringement accordingly.
outcome.remedy_or_orders: Declaration of infringement of fundamental rights under Article 12(1) and award of compensation.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 12(1) was central to the court's reasoning as it protects individuals from arbitrary state actions and guarantees equal protection under the law, which was directly violated by the unlawful police conduct in this case.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: The court found that the respondents failed to establish any factual basis for the arrests and searches, which were arbitrary and high-handed infringements of liberty and privacy, conducted without consent and reasonable suspicion.
